articles.title: A British man left his £180,000 estate to a diabetes charity in a will written on a frozen fish box and a mince pie packet; the High Court later ruled it was valid
articles.summary: A British man’s handwritten will, drafted on the cardboard packaging of a frozen fish box and a mince pie packet, has been ruled valid by the High Court,
articles.body: A British man’s handwritten will, drafted on the cardboard packaging of a frozen fish box and a mince pie packet, has been ruled valid by the High Court, clearing the way for a diabetes charity to inherit his estate worth approximately £180,000. Malcolm Roy Chenery, who lived in York, England, recorded his final wishes on two separate pieces of food packaging shortly before his death in May 2021. His estate included a three-bedroom house, money, jewellery and a large collection of ornaments and pottery. He named the British Diabetic Association, now known as Diabetes UK, as a principal beneficiary, while allocating his ornaments and pottery to the Hornsea Collector’s Society. The unusual format prompted legal questions over whether the two pieces constituted one valid will.How a frozen fish box and mince pie packet became a £180,000 willChenery wrote the first part of his will on the back of a Young’s frozen fish fillets box and the second on cardboard from a Mr Kipling mince pie packet. The pieces were small, measuring approximately 15 by 20 centimetres, and the writing appeared on their plain inner sides.The first piece, marked “1”, set out instructions concerning his house, bank accounts and household contents, which he wanted to leave to the “Diabetic Society”. It also specified that his ornaments and pottery should go to the Hornsea Collector’s Society.The second piece, numbered “2”, carried his signature and the date 3 May 2021. Two neighbours also signed it as witnesses that day. Chenery died the following day.What did the £180,000 estate include?The estate was valued at approximately £180,000 and included Chenery’s three-bedroom house, money, jewellery and personal possessions. His extensive collection of ornaments and pottery was another notable part of the estate.His handwritten instructions divided the intended gifts between Diabetes UK and the Hornsea Collector’s Society. The charity was the principal beneficiary, while the collectors’ society was named to receive the ornaments and pottery.The documents also recorded his wishes concerning his funeral. Chenery requested cremation and wanted his ashes buried or scattered at York Cricket Club, a place associated with happy memories of spending time there with his mother.Why did the unusual will end up in court?The dispute centred on whether the two pieces of cardboard could legally be treated as a single will. Although the documents were numbered consecutively and dealt with connected aspects of his estate, they came from different food packages.The neighbours who witnessed the second piece could not recall seeing the first when they signed. This raised questions about whether the two pieces together met the requirements for a valid will under English law.Diabetes UK sought to have both pieces admitted to probate as Chenery’s final will. If the court had rejected the documents, his estate would instead have been distributed under the rules governing intestacy, which apply when someone dies without a valid will.Why did the charity argue that the two pieces belonged together?The charity’s barrister, Sam Chandler, argued that the two pieces were part of the same document. Both had been written in the same pen, appeared to have been produced at the same time and contained overlapping subject matter.The claim also had support from members of Chenery’s family, some of whom explained that diabetes had affected relatives. This helped establish why the charity might have been a meaningful beneficiary for him.Although one sister had initially raised concerns about the circumstances, she later indicated that she would not actively oppose the claim and would leave the decision to the court. The case was therefore not simply a dispute between the family and the charity.What did the High Court rule?On 8 November 2024, Master Katherine McQuail of the High Court’s Chancery Division ruled that the two pieces of cardboard should be admitted to probate as Chenery’s last will.The court considered the requirements of the Wills Act 1837, including whether the documents could be treated as one testamentary document and whether the necessary formalities had been met. The judge accepted that the pieces were connected and reflected Chenery’s intention to distribute his possessions.The court also considered the principle that a person should not be presumed to have intended to die intestate when the evidence indicates a clear intention to make a will. It concluded that the two pieces should be admitted to probate, allowing the estate to pass in accordance with his wishes.The decision was reported in November 2024 and meant Diabetes UK could proceed with the legacy.You use AI every day. articles.title: Greece picks Embraer's C-390 transport aircraft: Why it matters for India's Rs 1 lakh crore IAF deal
articles.summary: Greece has become the latest European country to pick Embraer's KC-390 Millennium to modernise its air transport fleet.
articles.body: Greece has become the latest European country to pick Embraer's KC-390 Millennium to modernise its air transport fleet. The Hellenic Ministry of National Defense has signed a contract for three aircraft, with options for three more, through a government-to-government agreement between Greece and Portugal. The first aircraft is due in 2027 and will boost the Hellenic Air Force's airlift and air-to-air refuelling capabilities, while improving interoperability with NATO and allied forces.Greece is the seventh European nation to select the aircraft, after Portugal, Hungary, the Netherlands, Austria, the Czech Republic and Sweden. Outside Europe, it is operated by Brazil, South Korea, Uzbekistan, the UAE and Colombia. The aircraft carries 26 tonnes, cruises at up to 470 knots and can operate from temporary or unpaved runways. It handles cargo and troop transport, airdrops, medical evacuation, search and rescue, firefighting and humanitarian missions, and with quick-installation refuelling equipment it can work as both a tanker and a receiver.Why it matters for IndiaThe Greek order lands as India is shopping for the same class of aircraft. In August, the defence ministry floated a request for proposal worth close to Rs 1 lakh crore for 60 medium transport aircraft for the IAF. The programme is meant to replace the Soviet-era An-32 fleet, which has served for nearly four decades. More than 100 are still flying, each carrying around seven tonnes, from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to Eastern Ladakh. The RFP came two months after an An-32 crash at Jorhat killed five crew members. The new aircraft are also expected to take over some roles from the ageing Il-76, which carries about 45 tonnes.Three aircraft lead the field. Airbus' A400M Atlas carries 37 tonnes, the C-390 carries 26 tonnes, and Lockheed Martin's C-130J Super Hercules carries more than 20 tonnes. Only the C-130J is already in IAF service, and it has operated from high-altitude airstrips in Ladakh. The C-390 offers modern avionics, fly-by-wire controls and quick reconfiguration between missions. The A400M combines tactical and strategic airlift and can move heavy equipment, including armoured vehicles, from relatively short, unprepared runways.The stakes go beyond the IAF. Moving troops and equipment quickly along the borders with China in Eastern Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh has been a priority since the Galwan Valley clash, and a modern transport fleet would also strengthen the Army and the Navy. The aircraft would add to India's humanitarian assistance and disaster relief capability as well. The Greek contract shows the C-390 gaining ground among NATO and EU air forces, but India's choice will likely come down to payload, performance in its own terrain and how quickly the aircraft can enter service.

articles.title: A 57-year-old woman has been charged after police recovered dozens of keepsakes allegedly stolen from graves at a Milton cemetery; about 20 families reported missing lanterns, plants and memorial items
articles.summary: A lantern left beside a grave can be a reminder of someone who is no longer there.
articles.body: A lantern left beside a grave can be a reminder of someone who is no longer there. A potted plant can be a small act of care, while a candle can help a family feel connected to a loved one long after their death. For families visiting Milton Evergreen Cemetery in Ontario, Canada, some of these quiet gestures of remembrance reportedly turned into a distressing discovery when the objects they had left behind began disappearing. Now, a 57-year-old woman has been charged after police recovered dozens of items allegedly stolen from gravesites, with around 20 families reporting missing belongings.According to the Halton Regional Police Service, which announced the arrest on October 28, 2026, the alleged thefts began in late June. The cemetery contacted police in July after families reported that items placed near graves had gone missing. The recovered objects included items reported stolen as well as dozens of other belongings believed to have been taken from gravesites. The investigation has drawn attention to a painful distinction between the financial value of an object and what it means to the person who left it behind. For someone passing through a cemetery, a lantern or a plant might appear to be an ordinary possession. For a grieving family, however, it can be part of a deeply personal ritual of remembering someone they love.When the smallest keepsakes carry the biggest memoriesThe items reported missing from Milton Evergreen Cemetery included lanterns, shepherd hooks, candles, potted plants and other keepsakes placed near graves. Each belongs to a category of objects commonly used to personalise a gravesite, making a final resting place feel connected to the life and personality of the person being remembered. The police have not disclosed individual families' stories or the personal histories behind the missing objects, but the nature of the items highlights why such losses can be especially upsetting.In its statement, Halton Regional Police acknowledged that some of the objects might have relatively little monetary value while holding considerable sentimental importance for the people who placed them at their loved ones' graves. Recognising the personal impact of the alleged thefts, investigators made the case a priority. “While the monetary value of some of these items may be relatively low, many hold significant sentimental value for the families who placed them at their loved ones’ gravesite,” police said.Police recover dozens of items in MiltonThe investigation took a significant turn on October 24, when officers executed a search warrant at a residence in Milton. Police seized items that had been reported stolen, along with dozens of additional objects believed to have been taken from gravesites. On the same day, investigators arrested Diana Anderson, 57, of Milton. She has been charged with one count of theft under $5,000 and four counts of possession of property obtained by crime.The charges follow the investigation into the reported thefts at Milton Evergreen Cemetery. Police have not said that every recovered object has been linked to a particular family, and investigators are still working to catalogue the property and establish whether further victims were affected. Additional charges are anticipated, according to police. Investigators also believe some families may not yet have realised that items placed at their loved ones' graves have disappeared.The recovery of the objects could help investigators identify further victims and establish which belongings were taken from particular gravesites. For families who have already reported missing items, the process may also offer an opportunity to find out whether their personal tributes were among those seized.Police believe more families may be affectedHalton Regional Police have appealed to anyone who believes items were stolen from a gravesite at Milton Evergreen Cemetery in recent months to contact investigators. The appeal suggests that the number of affected families may not yet be fully known.Anyone who suspects that a memorial item has been taken can email investigators at PT1@haltonpolice.ca. People with information about the investigation can contact the 1 District Criminal Investigations Bureau at 905-825-4777, extension 2416.The investigation remains focused on identifying victims, documenting the recovered belongings and determining whether further charges are warranted. Anderson's charges are allegations, and the case has not established her guilt.At Milton Evergreen Cemetery, police are now working to return the story of these missing tributes to the families who may have lost them. As investigators continue to identify possible victims, the hope is that more of the recovered objects can be connected with the people who left them at gravesides in memory of someone they loved.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bengaluru daylight robbery: How robber used Fevikwik to glue woman receptionist's hands to desk, held her at knifepoint and fled with Rs 4.5L gold chain- video
articles.summary: BENGALURU: A knife-wielding robber stormed into a shoe and bag repair shop in Indiranagar, threatened to kill a woman employee, attacked her and snatched
articles.body: BENGALURU: A knife-wielding robber stormed into a shoe and bag repair shop in Indiranagar, threatened to kill a woman employee, attacked her and snatched her gold mangalya chain worth Rs 4.5 lakh in a daring daylight robbery on Oct 31.The accused, identified as Prabhuraj alias Raj, 40, had covered his head and face with a helmet and wore gloves. He also attacked the shop owner when he and members of the public tried to catch him before fleeing with the stolen chain.According to the complaint filed by Jayashree S, 23, a resident of Domlur, she has been working as a receptionist at Premium Shoe & Bag Repair on 100 Feet Road in Indiranagar for the past three years. The shop is owned by Ranjith Kumar. Her duties include receiving shoes and bags brought in by customers for repairs, issuing receipts and handing over the items to the workshop. She usually manages the shop's daily operations on her own.On Oct 31, Jayashree arrived at the shop around 10am and opened it for the day's work. Around 11.45am, an unidentified man wearing a helmet and gloves entered the shop. He suddenly jumped over the reception counter, where she was seated, and told her that someone was coming to kill him, warning her not to scream.Frightened, Jayashree tried to call Ranjith. However, Prabhuraj forcibly made her sit down, covered her mouth with his hands and pulled out a knife from his bag. He threatened to kill her if she raised an alarm and attacked her on the neck and hands with the knife.He then applied Fevikwik glue to both her hands to stick them to the desk and stuffed a piece of cloth lying on the desk into her mouth. He forcibly removed her gold mangalya chain, weighing around 35 grams and worth around Rs 4.5 lakh, from her neck and kept it in his pocket.When Prabhuraj attempted to flee, Jayashree managed to free her hands and screamed for help. Hearing her cries, members of the public rushed towards the shop. The accused then grabbed her by the hair, dragged her back inside and held a knife to her neck, warning those outside not to stop him.By then, Ranjith and others had reached the spot and tried to overpower him. Prabhuraj brandished the knife at them and attacked Ranjith before pulling Jayashree out of the shop and attempting to escape with the stolen chain.Members of the public and traffic police personnel present nearby chased the accused and caught him. Based on Jayashree's complaint, Indiranagar police registered a case under Section 309 (robbery) and arrested Prabhuraj.Deputy Commissioner of Police (East) Vikram Amathe said the woman was safe and had not sustained any injuries. He added that the accused appeared to be mentally disturbed and depressed. articles.title: Two Bristol teenage brothers build a £100 Braille printer inspired by their blind grandfather, win international award and plan to make the design free for everyone
articles.summary: Two brothers from Bristol have won international recognition for developing a portable Braille printer that can be built for around £100, offering a more
articles.body: Two brothers from Bristol have won international recognition for developing a portable Braille printer that can be built for around £100, offering a more affordable way to produce printed material for blind and partially sighted people. Tom Hunt, 19, and his younger brother Felix, 16, created the device, called BrailleGo!, after becoming aware of the difficulties people and organisations face in accessing Braille documents. Their grandfather, a Yorkshire-born engineer who contributed to the early development of the Jodrell Bank Observatory, lost his sight in his sixties, helping inspire their work. The brothers received the Best Start-Up Idea award at the 2026 World Robot Olympiad European Open Championship in Zagreb, Croatia. They now plan to release the printer’s design files, code and assembly instructions as an open-source project.How two Bristol brothers built a £100 Braille printerBrailleGo! is a compact device designed to produce short-run Braille documents, including children's books, museum guides, public information leaflets and meeting agendas. The brothers developed it under the team name Hunt Robotics, using readily available components and 3D-printed parts to keep the cost down.Commercial Braille embossers can cost more than £1,000 and may be bulky, making them difficult to access for individuals and smaller organisations with limited budgets. By contrast, the brothers estimate that BrailleGo! can be built for around £100.The printer is intended to address situations in which only a small number of Braille copies are needed. Rather than relying on expensive equipment for every printing requirement, organisations could potentially use a more affordable device to produce material for specific events, activities or visitors.Their grandfather's experience helped shape the ideaThe brothers' grandfather was an engineer from Yorkshire who contributed to the early development of the Jodrell Bank Observatory. He lost his sight in his sixties, giving the family a personal connection to the challenges faced by people living with sight loss.Their mother’s volunteering with the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB) also helped Tom and Felix understand the difficulties people and organisations can encounter when trying to access printed Braille material.These experiences encouraged them to explore how engineering could help make such resources more accessible. Their aim was not simply to build a working printer, but to develop one that people could reproduce without needing to invest in expensive specialist equipment.International recognition at the World Robot OlympiadThe brothers represented the UK at the 2026 World Robot Olympiad European Open Championship, held in Zagreb, Croatia, in October. Their project received the competition's Best Start-Up Idea prize.BrailleGo! also placed second in the Senior Future Innovators category, according to the competition's results. The event brought together 220 national-winning teams from 45 countries under the theme Robots Meet Culture, which challenged participants to explore how technology could improve access to arts, heritage and cultural experiences.The judging panel praised the printer's technical quality, including its 3D design and electronics, as well as the brothers' teamwork and focus on a real-world problem. Judges also noted that the pair had developed the device independently, without support from a coding or maker club.For Tom, who began studying Design Engineering at the University of Bristol in September, the recognition marked an important moment in a project that involved designing and building a machine capable of producing readable Braille.Why the brothers want to make the design freeInstead of focusing on commercialising BrailleGo!, Tom and Felix plan to make its code, design files and assembly instructions freely available as an open-source project. This would allow people in different communities to build the printer, adapt it to their needs and potentially improve the design.Making the plans available could help extend the idea beyond the brothers' own project, giving schools, community groups and organisations supporting people with sight loss an opportunity to explore a lower-cost approach to Braille printing.Tom said he hoped others would build on their work once the designs were shared. His younger brother Felix described the competition in Croatia as an opportunity to meet teams from around the world and learn from their projects, adding that building the printer had taught him about engineering, problem-solving and teamwork.Eleanor Southwood, director of impact and external affairs at sight-loss charity Fight for Sight, praised the concept, highlighting the potential uses of an affordable, portable printer for producing smaller quantities of Braille material.You use AI every day. articles.title: INS Vikrant gets a French touch: What changed aboard India's aircraft carrier for Rafale M
articles.summary: The Indian Navy's INS Vikrant, the first aircraft carrier built domestically, has undergone some changes as the ship prepares to induct the Rafale M.
articles.body: The Indian Navy's INS Vikrant, the first aircraft carrier built domestically, has undergone some changes as the ship prepares to induct the Rafale M. The first of the 26 naval variants of the fighter is scheduled to be inducted in the navy from 2028 onwards. Recently, the Rafale made its first landing on the INS Vikrant. Changes were made to the flight deck of the 45,000 tonnes ship, the largest of any warship made in India, ahead of the maiden landing of the aircraft on the sailing airbase. The Indian Navy has made a triangle landing aid on the ship, similar to the one found on the French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle.Why a carrier landing is so unforgivingA land runway runs to thousands of feet. A carrier's landing area is a fraction of that, and it sits on a deck that pitches and rolls with the sea. The jet comes in at roughly 240 kmph, and its tailhook has to catch one of the four arresting wires, which stops the aircraft in about one to two seconds. Pilots go to full power the moment the wheels touch down, so that if the hook misses the wires, a case known as a bolter, they can take off again and go around. Many of these landings are conducted at night or in poor weather, with pilots relying on the optical landing system and the landing signals officer who guides the pilot to stay on the right flight slope. The triangle marking is a supplementary visual reference for judging the approach and does not replace the optical landing system.The optical landing system is a key visual aide which guides the pilots on the prescribed glide path for the aircraft on to the desired touch point on the carrier. Th system projects light in such a manner that the pilot will only see the correct pattern of lights in the desired glide slope. Th lights will look improperly aligned if the aircraft is approaching either too shallow or too high, the system also provides visual cues for both these situations.What the first landing showedThe Rafale M landed on Vikrant on October 29, at the first attempt, a week after trials began at the shore-based test facility at INS Hansa in Goa, which recreates a carrier's ski-jump and arresting wires. It is part of a first flight campaign, and a second is planned next year.The jet was designed for the French carrier Charles de Gaulle, which launches aircraft with catapults. Vikrant has no catapult and uses a ski-jump for take-off, with arrested recovery for landing. The Rafale M's non-folding wings, about 10.9 metres across, also make movement between the deck, lifts and hangar harder, and work is under way to modify the lifts.India ordered 26 Rafale M jets for about Rs 63,000 crore in April 2025, with deliveries due from late 2028. The landing shows the ship and the aircraft can work together, but deck handling, maintenance and weapons integration still have to be proven before the jets are ready for operations.

articles.title: Meet Richard Andino, the nine-year-old California boy who turned two planter boxes into a successful vegetable business at his local farmers’ market in Loomis
articles.summary: Nine-year-old gardener and young entrepreneur Richard Andino, from Loomis in Placer County, California, has turned a simple school lesson about growing
articles.body: Nine-year-old gardener and young entrepreneur Richard Andino, from Loomis in Placer County, California, has turned a simple school lesson about growing plants into a thriving vegetable business. He started with two planter boxes, a handful of vegetables, and plenty of curiosity, driven by a lifelong love of vegetables and a desire to sell them. Three years on, his garden is nearly three times its original size, because it has grown a little bigger every year. On harvest days, he carefully checks which crops are ripe before preparing to serve customers, a routine that fills his summer holidays.How a family company and county approval took a boy’s vegetable stand to the Loomis Farmers MarketRichard’s first customers bought from a stand in front of his home. Today he is a regular vendor at the Loomis Farmers Market, a step that required his family to form a limited liability company and complete the county approval process for selling there, CBS News Sacramento reported.The money Richard earns covers summer activities such as Sky Zone and Sunsplash. Once he reaches his savings goal, he gives whatever remains of his harvest to members of the community.Why Richard would rather play outside than watch screens, and what his mother saw in kindergartenFor Richard, time outdoors matters more than the income. He told CBS News Sacramento that he is not a big fan of screens and would rather play outside.His mother, Kabryna Andino, told the same outlet that the preference grew out of his early school years. In kindergarten, she said, he began suffering from very bad migraines, which she linked to being indoors and watching too many screens.What a paediatrician says about screen time, sleep, mood and behaviour in today’s childrenRichard’s story comes as paediatricians continue to study how greater screen time affects children’s health. Amanda Mitchell, a paediatrician at Kaiser Roseville, told the outlet that heavy screen use changes the quality of children’s sleep, which in turn alters their mood and behaviour.She added that technology need not shape a whole generation. Children growing up in this era are overcoming its effects and becoming who they are meant to be, she said, and while technology helps them, it “does not define them”.Day to day, Richard tends the garden, talks with customers and grows something he built himself. He told the outlet that anyone who wants to run a business must expect challenges along the way. His advice is to keep going through each one, and success will follow.You use AI every day. articles.title: Best-selling author James Patterson has given more than $220 million to literacy and education, endowing over 1,000 scholarships; his giving now reaches students, teachers, libraries and independent bookseller
articles.summary: James Patterson is best known as one of the world’s most successful thriller writers, but his most consequential work may be happening far from the
articles.body: James Patterson is best known as one of the world’s most successful thriller writers, but his most consequential work may be happening far from the bestseller lists. Through a long-running commitment to literacy and education, Patterson has given more than $220 million to support readers, teachers, writers, libraries and independent booksellers, according to his official Giving Back page. His philanthropy has also endowed more than 1,000 scholarships at colleges and universities across the United States. The scale of that giving is unusual, but so is its breadth. Patterson’s support does not focus only on students or only on schools. It reaches the entire ecosystem that makes reading possible, from classroom teachers and librarians to authors, literacy researchers and the independent bookshops that connect communities with books. His stated belief is simple: reading changes lives, and better readers make better humans. Read more about his initiative here:A philanthropy built around readingPatterson’s approach begins with the idea that literacy is not a single issue but a chain of connected needs. A child needs effective reading instruction, a teacher needs training and resources, a school library needs books, a writer needs support and a local bookshop needs customers and stability. His giving reflects that understanding by funding people and institutions at every stage of the reading journey.The author has contributed more than $220 million to literacy-focused philanthropy to date, as per details on his official website. That figure includes grants and programmes for educators, writers, authors and librarians, as well as major support for literacy organisations and research-based reading instruction. The aim is not merely to distribute books, but to strengthen the conditions that help children become confident, capable readers.This focus is especially significant because reading ability shapes nearly every later opportunity in education and work. A student who struggles to read early can face widening difficulties in comprehension, confidence and academic progress. Patterson’s philanthropy therefore treats literacy as a long-term investment in opportunity rather than a short-term charitable gesture.Scholarships that change directionOne of the most visible parts of Patterson’s giving is his scholarship programme. He has endowed more than 1,000 scholarships at universities nationwide, giving students financial support to pursue higher education and careers in teaching, writing and public service.The scholarships include substantial support for historically Black colleges and universities. According to Patterson’s website, more than 600 scholarships have been endowed at HBCUs, making this one of the most important strands of his educational philanthropy. These awards can reduce financial pressure at a critical point in a student’s life and help more young people complete degrees that might otherwise be out of reach.The emphasis on teaching, writing and public service is also deliberate. By supporting students who may enter classrooms, newsrooms, public institutions or creative fields, Patterson is investing in the people who shape communities after they graduate. A scholarship is not only help with tuition; it can be the first step toward a career that creates further opportunity for others.Support for teachers and literacy researchPatterson has directed more than $50 million to educators, writers, authors and librarians through grants and programmes. This support recognises that teachers and librarians often work with limited budgets while carrying enormous responsibility for children’s learning and access to books.His giving also includes major donations to the University of Florida Literacy Institute, known as UFLI. The institute focuses on evidence-based reading instruction, an approach that uses research on how children learn to read in order to improve classroom outcomes. Patterson’s support for UFLI places his philanthropy alongside efforts to improve reading instruction at scale, rather than relying only on individual donations or one-time book giveaways, as per the website.That matters because reading instruction has become one of the most urgent issues in American education. Many children arrive at school without the foundational skills needed to read fluently, and teachers need practical, research-backed methods to help them catch up. By funding literacy research and instruction, Patterson’s giving aims to improve outcomes for children who may never know his name.Libraries and independent booksellersLibrarians occupy a central place in Patterson’s vision of literacy. They provide free access to books, internet access, study space and programmes for children and adults, often in communities where such resources are scarce. Patterson’s support for libraries acknowledges that a strong public reading culture depends on institutions that welcome everyone, regardless of income.Independent booksellers also receive a place in his giving. Patterson has provided more than $3 million in support to independent bookstores, businesses that often operate on narrow margins but play an outsized role in local literary life. They recommend books, host authors, support school partnerships and give readers a physical place to discover stories.This support is notable because independent bookshops compete with online retailers and large chains. Patterson’s grants recognise that a healthy literary culture is not created by publishers and authors alone. It also depends on the shops, libraries and local champions who put the right book into the right reader’s hands.Why Patterson’s giving stands outMany authors support literacy, but few have combined personal wealth, publishing influence and sustained giving at this scale. Patterson’s philanthropy is distinctive because it treats reading as a shared public project. It funds students, but also the educators, researchers, librarians and booksellers who make literacy possible every day.His approach also avoids treating books as a luxury. Patterson’s website frames reading as a pathway to opportunity, and his giving is designed to expand access for people who face financial or educational barriers. Whether through scholarships, teacher grants, library support or literacy research, the underlying goal is the same: help more people become readers and give them the tools to build better lives.There is also a practical lesson in the way the giving is structured. Rather than choosing one high-profile cause, Patterson has invested across the literacy system. That makes his philanthropy harder to summarise, but potentially more durable, because it strengthens the people and institutions that support readers long after a single grant or scholarship ends.A legacy beyond the bestsellersJames Patterson’s books have sold in enormous numbers, but his Giving Back page suggests that his longer-term legacy may rest on something quieter: children learning to read, students attending university, teachers receiving support and local bookshops staying open. More than $220 million has gone into that work, alongside more than 1,000 endowed scholarships and substantial support for HBCUs, literacy research, libraries and independent booksellers.The scale is remarkable, but the purpose is easy to understand. Patterson believes that reading changes lives, and his philanthropy is built to make that belief real for as many people as possible. In a world where access to books, good teaching and higher education remains uneven, his giving offers a model of how successful creators can use their resources to strengthen the foundations of opportunity.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
articles.summary: Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, a report has found.
articles.body:
The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found.

Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report.

The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic.

"This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation.

Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more.

So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage".

Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting.

'I was working 60 hours a week so I quiet quit'

The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults.

Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sunk to one-in-four, the lowest level on record.

In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%.

"Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added.

This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found.

Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade".

Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs".

"But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added.

articles.title: Stansted Airport workers spat at and racially abused - Unite
articles.summary: The scale of the abuse is laid bare in a survey of aviation workers across the UK.
articles.body:
Workers at London Stansted Airport have reported being spat at, assaulted and racially abused, according to a trade union.

The scale of harm was uncovered in a survey by Unite, which found 82% of workers at the Essex terminal were abused at least once a month.

Alcohol was the biggest trigger for abuse, followed by flight delays and baggage issues.

A Stansted spokesman said threatening or abusive behaviour was "completely unacceptable and will not be tolerated".

The figures obtained by Unite also found 27% of workers had been physically assaulted and 94% had witnessed a colleague being abused.

Unite extracted the data from a wider survey of 1,800 air transport staff across the UK.

Some of the respondents were not employed by Stansted but instead worked for airlines based there, including cabin crew and check-in staff.

"I have witnessed a colleague being spat at and a colleague being told, 'I hope you die on your way home in a car crash' and racially abused," said a Stansted security worker, speaking anonymously.

"On all occasions, the passengers have still been allowed to carry on with their journey."

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said abuse was not part of the job and urged airports and airlines to clamp down on the behaviour.

"All too often, these workers are being left in harmful positions while doing very difficult jobs," she added.

More than 29 million people fly from Stansted each year, making it the UK's fourth busiest airport.

Plans to increase its annual passenger numbers to 51 million by 2040 were approved in December .

The airport's spokesman said it worked closely with airlines, ground handlers, retailers, unions and the police to prevent and tackle inappropriate behaviour.

"We will continue to work hand-in-hand with all our partners, including our recognised trade unions, to ensure London Stansted Airport is a welcoming and safe place to work," he added.

In October, the government said it was working with airlines and trade unions to create a new system for sharing information on persistently disruptive passengers.

articles.title: Indian tourist killed after helicopters collide near Everest base camp
articles.summary: The two aircraft crashed just metres from the ground after trying to land at the same spot.
articles.body:
An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.

Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.

Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.

The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.

The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.

The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.

The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.

It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.

A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."

In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.

Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.

The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.

Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Kiren Rijiju on Tuesday slammed Rahul Gandhi after the Congress leader accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of becoming PM with “foreign help”.Taking a swipe at Rahul, Rijiju compared his remarks to Islamic fundamentalists speaking about secularism, separatists carrying Indian flags and anarchists displaying the Constitution.In a post on X, the minister said, “It's the same as islamic fundamentalists talking about secularism, separatists holding Indian flags & anarchists showing Constitution book. Pushing agendas of India's enemies yet accusing others of foreign support is self-ridiculing.”“Top level debates are done between matured people,” he added.Rijiju's remarks came a day after Rahul Gandhi launched an attack on the Prime Minister, alleging that he had become PM because of foreign support and continued to remain in office with such backing.Earlier in a post on X, the Congress leader alleged that PM Modi's financial system was controlled and supported by foreign interests and that foreign social media platforms backed him.“Mr Modi, stop lying to this nation,” Rahul said.“You became PM because of foreign help. Any stage, any time. Come if you have the guts. articles.title: Countdown record-breaker from Isle of Man reflects on dyslexia
articles.summary: Hazel Drury, from Ramsey, said winning eight shows had been "crazy".
articles.body:
A woman who won a record-breaking number of games on Countdown has described her success as "crazy", after once fearing dyslexia would hold her back.

Hazel Drury, from Ramsey, became the highest scoring woman to win eight consecutive episodes of the Channel 4 programme.

The 29-year-old was diagnosed with dyslexia when she was 15 and said it meant she struggled to complete her exams.

She said she "really wasn't expecting" her winning run and that it meant "so much" to her.

The daytime quiz show, first broadcast in 1982, is hosted by Colin Murray and is in its 94th series.

The Ramsey resident previously appeared on the programme at 18, winning four shows before eventually being knocked out.

According to the show's rules, contestants can reapply after 10 years, and Drury said it was her mother who persuaded her to return.

"When I was diagnosed at 15, it felt like the end of the world," she said.

"I just felt like I wouldn't be able to achieve anything and I was finding school really hard at the time."

Reflecting on becoming an "Octochamp" and scoring 1,000 points in a single run, she said: "It just means so much to me."

Drury, who has autism, said years of practice had helped her develop techniques to spot patterns in words and numbers.

"I think my brain's quite methodical," she said. "From all this watching and playing Countdown, something just clicked in my brain."

"The reaction from fans of the show and my colleagues, friends and family has been amazing," she added.

Drury will return to screens later this year when Countdown's quarter finals are broadcast in December.

articles.title: Europe on alert after bomb threats target at least four passenger flights
articles.summary: At least four passenger flights across Europe were targeted by suspected bomb threats on Tuesday, prompting emergency landings and security checks in
articles.body: At least four passenger flights across Europe were targeted by suspected bomb threats on Tuesday, prompting emergency landings and security checks in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria. All four aircraft landed safely, with counter-terrorism units and police deployed to inspect them. The incidents came a day after a separate bomb threat forced a Wizz Air flight from London to Sofia to divert to Budapest.In Poland, two separate flights were affected. A LOT Polish Airlines Boeing 737 MAX flying from London Heathrow to Warsaw Chopin Airport was diverted to Warsaw-Modlin after a bomb alert was received at 9.54 am local time. The aircraft landed at 10.01 am with 181 people on board, including a group of Jewish students aged 16 and 17 travelling from London on a school delegation. Passengers were evacuated and the aircraft moved to an isolated area for inspection. Modlin Airport was temporarily closed before resuming operations.A Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw also faced a bomb threat. The aircraft landed normally at Warsaw Chopin Airport and passengers disembarked, the airline said. Police took charge of the investigation, while airport operations continued.In Spain, a Ryanair flight from Manchester made an emergency landing at Murcia airport following another reported threat. The aircraft was carrying 121 people, including crew, according to Francisco Lucas, the Spanish government’s delegate in the Murcia region.In Bulgaria, a flight from Israel landed at Sofia airport after a bomb threat was received by email, Reuters reported, citing local media. Counter-terrorism units were deployed to check for possible explosive devices. The airport’s website showed an El Al service from Tel Aviv as the only flight arriving from Israel that morning. Bulgarian public broadcaster BNT said the alert was part of a wider warning affecting “various institutions”.The latest incidents follow a bomb threat on Monday involving a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia. The aircraft was diverted to Budapest and escorted by a Hungarian Gripen fighter jet. Wizz Air later said security checks had been completed and nothing suspicious was found.Several similar alerts involving flights to and from Israel were reported last month. An Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna was diverted to Sofia on October 18, while two Delta Air Lines flights faced separate bomb warnings earlier in the month. No explosives were found in those incidents, according to Ynet.Authorities have not established whether Tuesday’s threats were connected. Each alert was being treated as a security matter, with aircraft inspected and passengers evacuated or screened where required.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An Essex couple spent eight years building a miniature railway in their quarter-acre garden. It now has 400 metres of track and five locomotives, all outside their home
articles.summary: After they married in 2017, Dave Walker came up with an unusual project. He had a unique proposal for his wife, Angela.
articles.body: After they married in 2017, Dave Walker came up with an unusual project. He had a unique proposal for his wife, Angela. It wasn't a romantic getaway or a home upgrade, but a project that would give them plenty of time together while testing their patience and determination along the way. What was the project? Building a miniature railway in their garden!Angela, 55, and Dave, 54, have spent eight years working on a miniature railway running through their garden in Clacton-on-Sea, Essex. They dug the track beds themselves. Over the years, they collected memorabilia and accessories from around the world, and those pieces now give the line its character. Building a railway on this scale is slow, physical work, and the couple did most of it themselves.Four hundred metres on a quarter-acre plotThe railway runs for about 400 metres, or 1,312 feet, the BBC reported. That is, in fact, a lot of track for a quarter-acre plot, and it is laid with thousands of custom-made sleepers. Five locomotives run along the route. Miniature railways like this one are often lifelong projects for their owners, usually started in a field or a spare corner of the garden and extended over many seasons. The Walkers' version has reached a size that now defines the whole property."Our house is either now unsellable or worth triple. Most people think we're mental. They must think: 'Are they living the dream or are they mad?'" Dave told the Manchester Evening News. Regardless of what the world might think, the couple are glad they took on the project. "Our main strength is doing it together. Without each other, this would never have been built," Dave, who is also a DJ, told the broadcaster.The shared effort is indeed the beauty of this project. A railway that takes eight years to complete needs more than a good idea at the start. It needs two people who keep showing up for the digging, the collecting and the long weekends when the track is still just mud and sleepers. The Walkers have clearly found that partnership, and the result runs through their garden for everyone to see!"It is magic. I'm really pleased with what we've built. I wish I'd started it 20 years ago," Dave said.Angela shares her husband's enthusiasm for the unusual project. "We are not normal people; our house is not normal. It's not basic colours; we love it," she said. The miniature railway is certainly an attraction for any prospective buyer. The couple also have a more practical plan. They hope to use the railway to host fundraising events for the local lifeboat station, giving the project a purpose beyond the pleasure of owning it. Opening the garden to people from the community turns a private hobby into something the town can share.How much did this passion project cost the couple? articles.title: Trump's torment: From draining the swamp to drowning in mid-terms?
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent From Washington: Americans are streaming into polling stations across the country on Tuesday in one of the most consequential midterm
articles.body: TOI Correspondent From Washington: Americans are streaming into polling stations across the country on Tuesday in one of the most consequential midterm elections in modern U.S history, with Donald Trump facing the prospect of losing control of Congress and spending the final two years of a lame duck presidency negotiating with an opposition that has plenty of scores to settle. The MAGA boss used his closing campaign appearance rhapsodizing about the renovation of the Lincoln Reflecting Pool, a fittingly ironic finale to a campaign built around his promise to drain the swamp. By Tuesday night (Wednesday morning IST), if polls are correct -- and they often aren't -- he may discover that his own political fortunes are sinking.Trump's closing appearance was billed as a final midterm appeal to voters agitated by war and cost of living issues, but the 53-minute event often resembled a municipal contractor's presentation to a homeowners' association. Rather than delivering a reassuring economic and political argument, he walked his audience through the pool's renovation, complete with photographs, elaborate explanations of the plumbing issues, and some outright falsehoods, leaving political pundits slack-jawed at the tone-deaf approach to the elections where Republicans are on the backfoot.It was a bizarre climax to a campaign in which the MAGA supremo barnstormed roughly 20 states, addressing more than 30 rallies at which, in his own words, he “ranted and raved” in marathon two-hour speeches while treating congressional elections as a personal referendum despite asserting he is not on the ballot.Latest surveys suggests voters may be preparing to hand the President and his party a pasting, with one model by pollster Nate Silver giving Democrats roughly a 95 per cent chance of capturing the House and an 80 per cent chance of taking the Senate. Prediction market Kalshi has put Democrats winning the House at about 93 percent odds and taking the Senate at 71 percent.Headlines in major U.S newspapers include: "A terrible night awaits the GOP, and even that might be an understatement," "Democrats can’t believe their luck. No, really, they can’t" and "Five tell-tale signs of a Democratic blowout."However polls measure intentions, not votes. Republicans are counting on Trump's ability to mobilise his loyalists in the final hours, while Democrats are hoping that the discontent reflected in surveys translates into actual ballots. If, however, Republicans do lose both chambers as is being widely projected, Trump will enter the final two years of his presidency in territory familiar to three recent predecessors, though none approached the prospect with quite his combination of combativeness and appetite for confrontation.Barack Obama experienced the most recent equivalent after the 2014 midterms, when Republicans took the Senate and strengthened their House majority, leaving a Democratic President facing a Congress controlled entirely by the opposition. The result was legislative gridlock, with the most consequential episode coming in 2016, when Obama nominated Merrick Garland to the Supreme Court following Antonin Scalia's death. Senate Republicans, led by Mitch McConnell, refused even to schedule confirmation hearings, arguing that the vacancy should be filled by the next president. Garland's nomination expired without a vote.It was an extraordinary exercise of Senate power, with consequences that extended far beyond Obama's remaining months. Trump subsequently nominated Neil Gorsuch for the vacancy, and it ultimately helped reshape the Supreme Court for a generation.Similarly, George W. Bush ran into a Democrat-controlled House and Senate after the 2006 midterms, in the final two years of his presidency. The political backdrop was the deeply unpopular Iraq war, declining confidence in his administration and growing public dissatisfaction. Democrats used their congressional majorities to intensify oversight, challenge the administration's Iraq policy and push domestic legislation. Bush nevertheless negotiated on some issues, including the minimum wage and other measures, while foreign policy issues like the U.S-India nuclear deal found bipartisan support, demonstrating that divided government need not mean complete paralysis.Bill Clinton had perhaps the longest and most instructive experience of being hamstrung by a congressional opposition. After the 1994 "Republican Revolution," he faced the formidable speakership of Newt Gingrich in a relationship that was hardly cordial. It produced two government shutdowns in 1995-96, a succession of bruising legislative confrontations and, eventually, Clinton's impeachment in 1998. His political survival and high approval rating towards the end of his term demonstrated that an opposition-controlled Congress can sometimes become an opportunity for a president to reposition himself as a pragmatic centrist.No one is holding their breath about Trump adopting this course although he likes to present himself as a master deal-maker and negotiator. Past records and current form points to a man who prefers winning to finding compromises, and his instinct is to attack opponents, question their legitimacy, and turn political disagreements into personal vendettas. A Democratic Congress could therefore mean investigations, subpoenas, aggressive oversight of the administration and a near-constant battle over budgets, appointments and executive authority.You use AI every day. articles.title: Boy, 16, arrested over Halloween stabbings in Chandler's Ford
articles.summary: Five teenage boys, aged 16 and 17, were found with stab wounds at the party on Saturday night.
articles.body:
A third teenage boy has been arrested after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party.

Police said they were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to Park Road in Chandler's Ford , Hampshire, where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event.

One 17-year-old boy remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The others have been discharged from hospital.

A 16-year-old from Bristol has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. He remains in custody, as do two boys arrested on Monday.

Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.

One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'.

"And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."

Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.

Hampshire Police said officers were continuing to review video footage and information provided by witnesses to piece together the movements of those involved on the night.

Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie, senior investigating officer, said: "I want to thank everyone who has already come forward to speak about what they saw on the night, or share with us any footage they have.

"Our team are working incredibly hard to understand what happened and identify anyone who may have been involved.

"We now have arrested three boys, but we still want to hear from you if you have any information which could assist us. However small it may seem to you, it may be key to our enquiries."

The force said throughout the coming week, local officers from the Neighbourhood Policing Team are visiting local schools and colleges to offer further advice and reassurance, as well as to support those directly and indirectly affected by this incident.

Ch Insp Rachel Noble, district commander for Eastleigh, said: "The violence witnessed on Saturday night will have undoubtedly been extremely distressing and concerning for everyone who was at the party.

"It is really important to us that everyone knows what support is available for them, should they want to talk about, and how they can report anything to us so the investigation team can continue with their enquiries.

"Local officers will also continue to be out in the area of Park Road, so if you do have any concerns or need to speak about anything then do not hesitate to do so when you see them."

articles.title: Quincy Jones died in 2024, but his estate topped Forbes' 2026 highest-paid dead celebrities list at an estimated $150 million after selling music and media rights to HarbourView; Michael Jackson's estate ranked second
articles.summary: Quincy Jones spent more than seven decades shaping American music, film and television, and his influence is still generating extraordinary value after
articles.body: Quincy Jones spent more than seven decades shaping American music, film and television, and his influence is still generating extraordinary value after his death. Jones died of pancreatic cancer in November 2024 at the age of 91, yet Forbes has named his estate the highest-earning dead celebrity of 2026, with an estimated $150 million in earnings. The figure was driven largely by the sale of much of his music catalogue and related rights to HarbourView Equity Partners in March.The result is a reminder that creative ownership can become a lasting financial asset. Jones’s estate did not simply earn royalties from old recordings. It sold a portfolio that included his personal catalogue, publishing rights and interests in a career that touched Michael Jackson, Frank Sinatra, Ray Charles, Aretha Franklin, television and film. Forbes estimates that the HarbourView transaction was worth around $150 million, placing Jones ahead of Michael Jackson’s estate, which earned an estimated $140 million. Read more details about it here:Why Jones topped the listJones’s career was unusually broad. He worked on Michael Jackson’s Thriller, Frank Sinatra’s 'Fly Me to the Moon', and music associated with Ray Charles, Donna Summer, Miles Davis, Count Basie and Aretha Franklin. He also co-founded Vibe magazine, executive produced The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, conducted 'We Are the World', and received two Oscar nominations for scoring Steven Spielberg’s 'The Color Purple'. That range made his rights valuable in more than one market. In March 2026, his estate sold the vast majority of its interests in those assets, along with Jones’s personal catalogue and publishing rights to songs including 'Soul Bossa Nova', to HarbourView Equity Partners. Forbes estimates the deal at approximately $150 million and treats that transaction as the main reason Jones leads this year’s list.Industry insiders told Forbes that Jones’s estate secured a premium price because the assets generate ongoing revenue and because his reputation carries commercial weight. HarbourView also gains the prestige of owning rights connected to one of music’s most respected producers, which may help the firm pursue future catalogue acquisitions.The Michael Jackson connectionA key part of Jones’s financial story remains tied to Michael Jackson. Jones held a 10 percent producer royalty on Jackson’s first three solo albums, Off the Wall, Thriller and Bad. Forbes reports that those albums account for more than two-thirds of Jackson’s annual global streaming total, giving Jones’s estate a powerful recurring income stream.That connection became especially lucrative in 2026. The Michael biopic became a global box-office hit, grossing more than $1 billion worldwide, and the film’s success boosted interest in Jackson’s catalogue and related projects. Jones’s producer royalties therefore paid out substantially at the same time his estate was negotiating the HarbourView sale.The timing helped Jones take the top spot. Forbes notes that this is only the fourth year since Michael Jackson’s death in 2009 that another deceased celebrity has led the list, with each exception involving a major asset sale. The other three were Elizabeth Taylor in 2012, Roald Dahl in 2021 and J.R.R. Tolkien in 2022.Michael Jackson’s estate ranks secondMichael Jackson’s estate earned an estimated $140 million over the past year, according to Forbes. The estate invested an estimated $25 million to fund reshoots for the Michael biopic, a gamble that paid off when the film grossed more than $1 billion globally.Forbes estimates that the estate will eventually receive about 25 percent of the film’s net profits, amounting to more than $50 million over the coming years. The movie also lifted the wider Jackson business portfolio, including music streaming, the Cirque du Soleil show in Las Vegas, productions of MJ: The Musical, and brand licensing. Together, those businesses generated $140 million over the 12 months covered by Forbes’ ranking. The estate’s result shows how a single successful film can strengthen an entire posthumous brand, increasing streaming, ticket sales and licensing revenue across multiple markets.How the ranking worksForbes’ 2026 list measures pre-tax earnings from sales, streams, licensing deals and other income sources between October 1, 2025 and September 30, 2026. It also includes estate acquisitions made or announced during that period.This year’s methodology treats each celebrity as a single entity and credits all income generated, regardless of whether beneficiaries still own or control the rights to the person’s work, name, image or likeness. That is a change from the 2025 list, which focused on money flowing to estate beneficiaries. Forbes compiled its figures with data from Luminate and interviews with industry insiders, and it does not deduct agent, manager or lawyer fees.The methodology explains why a major catalogue sale can dominate the list. A one-time transaction can produce a far larger figure than annual royalties, even when the underlying catalogue continues to earn steadily year after year.The wider dead-celebrity economyJones and Jackson lead a list that shows how celebrity estates increasingly operate like media companies. Dr. Seuss ranked third with an estimated $80 million, followed by Elvis Presley at $75 million and Dolly Parton at $46 million. Each estate relies on a mix of music, publishing, licensing, live experiences and brand extensions.Physical destinations remain especially important for some estates. Graceland continues to draw hundreds of thousands of visitors each year, while Dollywood attracted 3.4 million visitors in 2025, an 8 percent increase in a year when many American theme parks saw attendance decline. These locations act as hubs for merchandise, tourism and brand expansion.Still, Forbes cautions that success is not guaranteed. Bob Marley’s Las Vegas stage production closed after a brief hiatus in January, while Bruce Springsteen’s film Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere underperformed at the box office. The lesson is that valuable intellectual property helps, but every new film, show or licensing venture still carries risk.A legacy measured in influence and incomeQuincy Jones’s place at the top of Forbes’ 2026 list is not simply a story about money. It reflects the enduring value of work that continues to reach audiences decades after it was created. His catalogue, production royalties and media interests became valuable because his creative fingerprints remain embedded in some of the most successful music and entertainment of the past half-century.Michael Jackson’s estate ranks close behind, proving that a global hit film can still reshape the economics of a legacy brand. But Jones’s $150 million result shows something broader: in today’s entertainment economy, ownership of songs, publishing rights and creative history can be as valuable as a new release.You use AI every day. articles.title: The Texas test: Latino voters could make or break Trump's midterms
articles.summary: Latino voters are emerging as one of the most closely watched constituencies in the US midterm elections, with their choices potentially influencing the
articles.body: Latino voters are emerging as one of the most closely watched constituencies in the US midterm elections, with their choices potentially influencing the outcome of key races in Texas and offering a broader indication of how US president Donald Trump’s 2024 gains among Hispanic voters are holding up.In Texas, where Latinos account for nearly a third of the eligible electorate, a shift in their support could have consequences for the closely contested Senate and gubernatorial races, as well as several competitive House districts.The political significance extends beyond Texas. Competitive congressional districts in California, Arizona, Florida and Pennsylvania also have substantial Latino populations, meaning even modest changes in voting preferences could affect the balance of power in the House of Representatives. The results could also help establish whether the Republican gains among Latino voters in 2024 represented a lasting political shift or a temporary movement driven by the issues and candidates of that election.Why the Latino vote matters in TexasTexas has nearly 6.3 million eligible Latino voters, accounting for about 31.7% of the state's eligible electorate, according to the UCLA Latino Policy and Politics Institute.Their numbers were influential in 2024, when Trump won approximately 55% of Hispanic voters in Texas, according to exit polls. He also carried several South Texas counties that had voted Democratic in 2020.Those shifts helped Republicans redraw the state's political map with greater confidence after the 2024 election. Texas Republicans' mid-decade redistricting push, carried out at Trump's urging, sought to improve their prospects in several congressional districts where the president had performed strongly. But a change in Latino voting preferences could complicate that strategy.The region is already central to several competitive House contests. Republican Rep Monica De La Cruz is facing Democrat Bobby Pulido, while Democratic Rep Vicente Gonzalez is running against Republican Eric Flores. The races are being fought in districts where Latino voters form an important part of the electorate.What could bring Latino voters back towards Democrats?Economic concerns and immigration enforcement are emerging as key issues shaping the vote, though strategists disagree on which matters more.According to CBS News, Trump's approval rating among Latinos stood at 24% in early October. Among those who voted for him in 2024, approval had fallen to 57%, from 93% in February 2025. An October CBS poll also found that 51% of Latino voters planned to support a Democratic House candidate, compared with 24% for a Republican.Democratic strategist Chuck Rocha attributed the discontent largely to rising prices, fuel costs and affordability, with immigration enforcement adding to concerns in South Texas. He described Latino voters as increasingly willing to move between parties, calling the shift “dealignment” rather than a permanent realignment.Texas Democratic Rep Joaquin Castro, however, sees immigration enforcement as the bigger factor. He told CBS News that ICE operations had directly affected Latino communities, particularly Hispanic men, who felt they were being treated collectively as criminals.“I think it's mostly because of ICE and how they have targeted the Latino community in Texas and across the country,” Castro said.Latino voters are not a politically uniform group; their priorities vary across rural and urban communities, age groups, gender and occupation.The polling picture — and its limitsPolling suggests Democrats have an opening in the state's major contests. An October CBS News poll found that six in 10 Hispanic voters planned to support Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton in the Senate race. Latino voters also favoured Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa over incumbent Republican Gov Greg Abbott by a similar margin.A University of Houston Hobby School survey found Talarico leading Paxton among Latino voters statewide, 52% to 41%. But the breakdown by geography showed a more complicated picture: rural Latino voters favoured Paxton, 56% to 24%, while urban Latino voters backed Hinojosa over Abbott, 58% to 41%.Decision Desk HQ's average of Hispanic polling data also showed Talarico leading Paxton by more than 20 percentage points among Latino voters, a swing of roughly 30 points towards Democrats compared with Trump's performance among the group in 2024.Republicans have questioned whether the apparent shift will translate into votes. Republicans argue that Democrats had yet to persuade many Latino men, particularly those working in energy, law enforcement and federal agencies, that the party's economic and immigration policies would serve their interests.They also point to the role of religion and conservative social views among some Hispanic voters, arguing that Republicans had built a higher baseline of support over the past decade.Turnout could be as important as preferenceThe number of Latino voters who turn out could prove as important as which candidates they support.Nearly 150,000 voters cast early ballots in Hidalgo and Cameron counties during the first week of voting, a 63% increase over the comparable period in the 2022 midterms, according to figures reported to the Texas Secretary of State's office. The rise points to greater participation in heavily Hispanic South Texas, but does not indicate which party those voters favour.The region has also shown a history of ticket-splitting. In 2024, Trump carried Hidalgo County even as Democratic House candidates Michelle Vallejo and Vicente Gonzalez won majorities there, suggesting voters may back different parties in statewide and congressional contests.An analysis by Equis cautioned against treating primary turnout as a reliable predictor of general-election results, particularly in heavily Latino counties where Democratic primaries can decide some local races. It found that Talarico won 54% of the two-way vote in majority-Latino precincts in major urban counties, 67% in the Rio Grande Valley and 63% in the Upper Rio Grande region near El Paso during the Democratic Senate primary. But the group warned that these figures cannot establish how the same voters will behave in the midterms.Campaigns are competing for voters who cannot be taken for grantedDemocrats have invested more heavily in Latino outreach this cycle, moving beyond the practice of translating English-language campaign advertisements into Spanish only in the final weeks of an election. Campaigns have sought to reach voters through Spanish-language programming, social media influencers and messengers with established community connections.Talarico's campaign spent $800,000 on World Cup advertising, including Spanish-language spots, while Hinojosa's campaign placed an advertisement during a boxing match featuring Mexican star Canelo Álvarez.Republicans, meanwhile, are seeking to retain the support they gained in 2024 by emphasising the economy, border security, faith and family values. Trump has defended his record with Hispanic voters, pointing to falling poverty rates among Hispanic Americans and arguing that Democratic policies would threaten economic growth and border security.What the result could mean beyond TexasThe Texas vote will be watched well beyond the state's borders because it could offer an indication of whether Latino voters are continuing to move between the parties rather than settling into a durable political alignment.A Democratic recovery among Latino voters could complicate Republican efforts to hold competitive House districts in states such as California, Arizona, Florida and Pennsylvania, where sizable Latino electorates can influence close races. It could also give Democrats a template for reaching voters who supported Trump in 2024 but have since become dissatisfied with his administration.But a strong Democratic performance in Texas would not, by itself, establish that Latino voters have permanently shifted back towards the party.For Republicans, retaining the support they won in 2024 will depend on whether their candidates can address voters' concerns about prices, immigration enforcement and the economy. For Democrats, the task is to convert dissatisfaction into sustained support while persuading voters who remain sceptical of the party.For now, Texas is a test of how much either party can rely on an electorate that has shown it is willing to move.You use AI every day.
