articles.title: Jury in Russell Brand rape trial begins considering verdicts
articles.summary: The media personality has been on trial for three weeks, after pleading not guilty to all charges.
articles.body:
The jury has begun considering the verdicts in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault trial.

The media personality, 51, has been on trial at Southwark Crown Court in London for three weeks, facing three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.

He has pleaded not guilty to all the charges. Giving evidence, he told the court he had been "obsessed" with sex in the past, but insisted it was always consensual.

The charges relate to allegations from six women spanning a decade between 1999 and 2009. Prosecutors said the complainants described him as someone who "didn't listen" when they said no, and "didn't care".

On Tuesday, judge Mr Justice Bennathan told the jury of eight men and four women he can only accept a verdict they all agree on.

Brand was one of the UK's most high-profile comedians, presenters and actors during the 2000s.

At the trial, he admitted using his fame to "facilitate sexual access", which he now said was wrong, but denied ever doing anything criminal.

His barrister told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".

He also said none of the women reported the alleged incidents to police at the time, and that allegations in a 2023 TV and newspaper investigation had "poisoned the well of justice" by prompting women to come forward afterwards.

Meanwhile, prosecutors depicted Brand as someone who saw women as a "disposable commodity" who "didn't matter to him" and were simply a "means to an end".

Barrister Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told the jury that the women said his personality changed "from charming to frightening to nasty" during the alleged attacks.

She said the women, who do not know each other, had been "haunted for years" by their experiences.

One woman accuses Brand of raping her after they had met at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.

She claimed he turned from "camp, friendly and effeminate" to "monster-like" before the alleged assault.

When asked if there was any truth in the allegations that he raped her, he told the court: "No."

Another woman claims that the entertainer grabbed her breasts at a bar in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet, where he allegedly orally raped her.

Brand said he remembered going into the toilet with the woman but did not drag or force her there, or force her to perform oral sex.

A third woman had a consensual sexual encounter with Brand and another fan in his dressing room at the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London in 2009.

She accuses the star of later raping her after he invited her to his house in Hampstead.

She said she had agreed to vaginal sex but did not consent to anal sex. After he texted her six months later, she said she told him he had "treated me like an animal".

Brand told the court they had consensual sex, and denied committing anal rape.

The other allegations come from a woman who says she was pinned against a wall and groped; another who claims he put his head into her lap when she had been forced to give him a massage; and a complainant who says he tried to drag her into a toilet. Brand also denies these charges.

Brand's wife Laura gave evidence in his defence at the trial, describing him as "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".

Allegations of sexual misconduct against Brand were first made in a Channel 4 documentary and a Times and Sunday Times investigation in 2023.

He denied those allegations, which related to different women than those involved in the criminal trial.

Brand first rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. He was married to pop star Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.

In recent years Brand has reinvented himself as an online social, political and religious commentator.

articles.title: Meet Eva Outram, UK woman who quit her $58,000 NHS job after surviving 23 days in the wilderness; now lives in a caravan, teaches outdoor skills and saves $3,200 a month
articles.summary: Meet Eva Outram, UK woman who quit her $58,000 NHS job after surviving 23 days in the wilderness; now lives in a caravan, teaches outdoor skills and saves
articles.body: Meet Eva Outram, UK woman who quit her $58,000 NHS job after surviving 23 days in the wilderness; now lives in a caravan, teaches outdoor skills and saves $3,200 a monthFor 23 days, Eva Outram lived in the Canadian wilderness, where finding food, surviving without modern comforts and dealing with isolation became part of her daily routine. But when the 28-year-old British woman returned home from the survival reality show 'Alone', it was not the wilderness she wanted to leave behind. Instead, she began questioning the life she had built around a steady job, a mortgage and the expectation that success meant settling into a conventional routine. She eventually quit her $58,000-a-year job with the UK's National Health Service (NHS), moved into a caravan with her partner and embraced a life centred on outdoor adventures. Today, the couple say they save around $3,200 every month.According to reports by PEOPLE, Outram had been working as an NHS project manager and living in a two-bedroom flat in Leeds, England. Her annual salary was about $58,000, but mortgage payments, bills and other living expenses left her feeling as though she was working primarily to maintain her lifestyle.Her experience on 'Alone', a Channel 4 survival series in which contestants attempt to survive in a remote part of Canada, became a turning point. After spending 23 days in the wilderness, she returned with a different perspective on what she wanted from life.From an NHS career to a life outdoorsOutram had followed a familiar path: getting an education, finding a stable job and buying a home. She purchased her Leeds flat in October 2022, but the financial commitments associated with it soon began to feel restrictive. “I had always had an inkling that the traditional way of living wasn't for me, but I was on the conveyor belt of going to university and getting a good job,” she told PEOPLE. She described spending a year in the flat feeling as though she was on a “hamster wheel” of working to pay the mortgage. Her appearance on 'Alone' gave her an opportunity to step away from that routine and examine the choices she had made. The experience also brought her closer to the outdoors, where everyday comforts were no longer guaranteed and survival depended on resourcefulness.In a 2024 interview with outdoor retailer Valley and Peak, Outram described her time on the show as an exceptionally difficult experience. She said she had little survival experience before participating, beyond spending a couple of years in the Scouts as a child. Foraging for food, dealing with isolation and living without running water or proper shelter tested her in ways that ordinary city life had not. She recalled going days with little more than handfuls of berries to eat.After returning to the UK, she felt a strong desire to change almost every aspect of her life. She left her NHS job and began pursuing her interest in outdoor activities and wilderness skills.A £4,800 caravan becomes her new homeOutram's transition to caravan living was not entirely unfamiliar. Her partner, Tom Park, 33, a stonemason, had already been living in a caravan when they met. She often spent weekends with him and gradually became attracted to the freedom his lifestyle offered. In August 2024, Outram began renting out her Leeds flat, and the couple bought a caravan together for £4,800, approximately $6,100 according to AS USA.The caravan became their full-time home, allowing them to move away from the substantial accommodation expenses associated with conventional housing. Instead of paying rent, they stay on farmland in exchange for helping with work around the properties. Their responsibilities vary according to where they are staying. At one farm, they helped with general maintenance and looked after chickens, while Park also undertook construction work. At their current location, which welcomes children and visitors, Outram spent two weeks doing face painting.The arrangement means the couple can receive accommodation, electricity and water in exchange for a few hours of work each week. Outram told PEOPLE that the work generally involves just a handful of hours, while reports put their weekly commitment at around three to six hours. They have not abandoned work altogether. Outram earns money through content creation and outdoor-related ventures, while Park continues to undertake paid work.How they save around $3,200 every monthThe financial difference between their former and current lifestyles is substantial, according to Outram's account. Before moving into the caravan, their reported monthly expenses included a mortgage of about £800, ground rent of £150, bills of £315 and food expenses of approximately £40. Together, these amounted to around £1,305 a month.Under their current arrangement, they have no accommodation costs, and the farm provides electricity and water. Their reported regular expenses include gas costing about £40 every few months and a weekly food shop of approximately £85. Outram and Park estimate that they can save around £2,500 each month, equivalent to roughly $3,200 at the exchange rate used in AS USA's report. The figure represents their combined savings rather than Outram's individual earnings.“We have a total sense of freedom,” Outram said, according to a report by the Yorkshire Post. She added that the arrangement gives them higher disposable income and allows them to decide how to use their money without being tied to a single location.Their reduced expenses have also given Outram greater flexibility to pursue her interests in the outdoors. Through The Grim Adventure Club, she has explored opportunities to offer bushcraft and wilderness workshops, hiking and canoeing expeditions, with the aim of helping other people develop a closer connection with nature.Saving for a home while choosing freedomDespite moving away from conventional homeownership, Outram and Park have not abandoned the idea of having a permanent place of their own. They hope to save enough money to purchase a plot of land and build a home, or buy a rundown property they can renovate. For now, however, they have no immediate plans to return to the housing arrangements they left behind. Their lower living costs have allowed them to save while continuing to explore different places and outdoor experiences.In an interview with the Yorkshire Post, Outram said the assumption that people living this way must be struggling financially was misleading in their case. She said she had earned more than ever before and had no intention of returning to her previous lifestyle. “I genuinely feel like I am living my dream life,” she said, according to AS USA.You use AI every day. articles.title: FIVE to play Chelmsford's Central Park for second annual festival
articles.summary: The boyband are hoping everybody gets up for their visit to the Essex county town.
articles.body:
FIVE have been announced as the first headline act for a festival in Essex next year.

Despite recent performances in Australia and New Zealand, the 1990s boyband are due to keep on movin' for the second annual Chelmsford Summer Series in the city's Central Park on 27 August.

It will mark 30 years since their formation and follows the band's reunion in 2025.

Jennie Lardge, the deputy leader at Chelmsford City Council, said the festival "reflects our ambition for the city".

"[They are] also helping to strengthen Chelmsford's reputation as a destination for culture and events that the whole city can be proud of," said the Liberal Democrat councillor, who is also cabinet member for culture and leisure.

FIVE sold more than 20 million records in the late 1990s and early 2000s with tracks such as When The Lights Go Out, If Ya Gettin' Down and Slam Dunk (Da Funk).

The quintet appeared together on stage for the first time in more than 25 years for their Keep On Movin' tour of the UK and Ireland in 2025.

Chelmsford Summer Series is run by promotions company Louder Entertainment. McFly, Sugababes and Craig David performed at the inaugural event this summer.

A spokesperson said further artists and details would be announced.

Chelmsford has not hosted a major flagship music festival since the final V Festival in 2017, but has enjoyed a renaissance of events in recent years, with the inaugural State Fayre at Hylands Park this summer and BBC Radio 2 in the Park in 2025 .

articles.title: Asda hires former Morrisons boss David Potts in bid to grow firm
articles.summary: David Potts takes charge of Asda, which is based in Leeds, with immediate effect.
articles.body:
Asda has appointed a former Morrisons boss as chief executive to help lead revival efforts at the supermarket chain.

Asda, which is based in Leeds, said David Potts would take on the role with immediate effect, while current boss Allan Leighton would become non-executive chairman, two years after returning to lead the supermarket chain.

Potts led Morrisons from its Bradford headquarters for eight years until 2023, overseeing a turnaround during which the supermarket chain was bought by US private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice.

Potts said Asda had "made good progress but significant opportunities remain" to reinvigorate sales, with a focus on keeping prices low for shoppers.

"By making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues," he said.

Before joining Morrisons, Potts was chief executive of Tesco's Irish business, its UK arm and its Asian operation.

According to Asda, Leighton had planned to step aside from the day-to-day running of the group, after he returned in 2024, more than two decades after serving as chief executive.

"Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth," said Leighton.

"David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him."

Last year, issues with an IT upgrade hit product availability at the supermarket and dented sales, impacting its bottom line.

But in August, it reported sales had returned to growth for the current quarter for the first time in two years.

articles.summary: Trichy international airport numbers arrival terminal pillars 1–9 at new integrated terminal, helping passengers share pickup points and easing traffic chaos.
articles.body: Trichy: Passengers arriving at Trichy international airport will now find it easier to share their location with cab drivers or people coming to pick them as Airports Authority of India (AAI) has numbered the pillars at the arrival terminal of the new integrated terminal building. All pillars from 1 to 9 on both sides facing the terminal and the cityside have got numbers now.So far, passengers coming out of the terminal have been having a tough time sharing their exact location near the carriageway with those coming to pick them. Peak-hour crowds and high movement of cars, often chaotic, make it difficult for passengers as well as drivers to locate each other. The airport management said passengers can now have hassle-free coordination with their drivers by referring the numbered pillars.
